original_question: For a sequence of integers (x_n) and a fixed digit k, define U_n^(k) to be the position of the digit k in x_n when k occurs and 0 otherwise. Study the sequence U_n^(k) when x_n is the nth prime, n!, or n^n, including questions of convergence and monotonicity, and determine whether these digit-position sequences contain infinitely many prime numbers. Ask the same questions more generally for rational sequences.
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problem 21: the digit-position sequence U_n^(k) attached to a fixed digit k and a sequence (x_n), with the specific cases x_n = p_n, x_n = n!, and x_n = n^n, and with a final extension to rational sequences. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's actual target. It correctly identifies the position sequence attached to a fixed digit k, the three special families x_n = p_n, x_n = n!, and x_n = n^n, the two qualitative properties explicitly named in the paper ('convergence' and 'monotony'), the question of whether the position sequence contains infinitely many prime values, and the closing extension from integer sequences to rational sequences. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
missing_details: The paper's official target is specifically Unsolved Problem 21, not a broader problem about digit statistics in arbitrary sequences. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

The paper treats k as a decimal digit; a stand-alone question should say so explicitly. The example uses ordinary base-10 numerals such as 5, 17, and 715. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
The notation p_n should be defined explicitly as the n-th prime. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

A stand-alone version should spell out the indexing convention for 'position'. In the paper's example, x_2 = 17 gives U_2^(7) = 2 and x_3 = 715 gives U_3^(7) = 1, which is the convention your rewrite should preserve if you want to stay closest to the scanned arXiv formulation. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/333540693/Florentin-Smarandache-Thirty-Six-Problems-in-Number-Theory-pdf?utm_source=openai))

The default value when k does not occur should be stated explicitly; in the scanned paper this value is 0. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/333540693/Florentin-Smarandache-Thirty-Six-Problems-in-Number-Theory-pdf?utm_source=openai))

The original wording does not resolve what happens if k occurs more than once in x_n; this is an implicit gap in the paper itself, and your draft also leaves it implicit. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

For the rational-sequence extension, the paper says only 'when {x_n} is a sequence of rational numbers'; a stand-alone formulation should at least say that the same digit-position rule is to be interpreted via decimal expansions, while noting that the paper does not specify how terminating versus repeating expansions are to be handled. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

To remain paper-faithful, the scope should stop at convergence, monotony, and infinitude of prime values in the position sequence; it should not be broadened to asymptotic digit frequencies, normality, or other distributional questions. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
refined_question: Let k be a fixed decimal digit, and let (x_n)_{n\ge 1} be a sequence of integers. Define the position sequence (U_n^(k)) by setting U_n^(k) = i if k is the i-th digit of the decimal expansion of x_n, and U_n^(k) = 0 if the digit k does not occur in x_n; in particular, the paper's example gives U_2^(7) = 2 for x_2 = 17 and U_3^(7) = 1 for x_3 = 715. For x_n = p_n, where p_n is the n-th prime, and likewise for x_n = n! and x_n = n^n, determine whether the sequence (U_n^(k)) converges, whether it is monotone, and whether it contains infinitely many prime terms; then ask the same questions, with the same digit-position convention, when (x_n) is a sequence of rational numbers. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/333540693/Florentin-Smarandache-Thirty-Six-Problems-in-Number-Theory-pdf?utm_source=openai))
justification: The draft is already a near-paraphrase of the paper's Unsolved Problem 21, so the right refinement is to keep it narrow and not replace it with any neighboring digit problem. I therefore retained exactly the three model sequences named in the paper, exactly the three questions the paper asks about them (convergence, monotony, and whether infinitely many prime values occur in the position sequence), and the paper's final extension to rational sequences. The main sharpening was to make explicit the role of p_n and to encode the paper's position convention by repeating its own example. I did not invent alternate variants, and I treated the multiple-occurrence issue as a missing detail rather than silently changing the problem. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
